judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v ABU BAKAR BIN IBRAHIM
judgments.catchwords: Setelah menilai keseluruhan keterangan, Mahkamah mendapati bahawa terdapat keraguan yang munasabah terhadap persoalan asas sama ada OKT mempunyai “custody” atau “control” terhadap dadah yang ditemui: (i) Mahkamah menerima bahawa bilik tersebut mempunyai kaitan dengan OKT. Mahkamah juga menerima bahawa SP1 hingga SP4 berada di premis atas kebenaran OKT. Walau bagaimanapun, keadaan tersebut tidak mencukupi untuk menutup jurang dalam keterangan mengenai “custody” atau “control” terhadap dadah. (ii) Keterangan mengenai kedudukan OKT ketika tangkapan bercanggah dengan keterangan lain dan menimbulkan keraguan sama ada OKT berada di dalam bilik ketika dadah ditemui. Dalam keadaan terdapat empat (4) orang lain di premis tersebut, Mahkamah tidak dapat menyatakan dengan yakin bahawa OKT dan bukannya orang lain mempunyai “custody” atau “control” terhadap dadah. (iii) Mahkamah dengan itu tidak bersetuju dengan hujahan Pendakwaan bahawa keadaan-keadaan tersebut secara kumulatif sudah memadai untuk membentuk kes prima facie. Sebaliknya, Mahkamah mendapati bahawa kes Pendakwaan bergantung kepada suatu inferens yang memerlukan Mahkamah membuat andaian terhadap fakta yang masih bercanggah. (iv) Mahkamah juga tidak bersetuju bahawa fakta premis / bilik tersebut dikaitkan dengan OKT dengan sendirinya membawa kepada “possession”. Sebagaimana yang ditegaskan, “possession” memerlukan unsur fizikal dan mental, dan “animus possidendi” hendaklah disimpulkan daripada keadaan sekeliling. Dalam kes ini, keadaan sekeliling yang telah dibuktikan tidak menghasilkan suatu inferens yang selamat mengenai “custody”, “control” dan animus possidendi. Sebaliknya, percanggahan keterangan menimbulkan suatu keraguan yang material terhadap elemen tersebut. (v) Dalam Goh Ming Han (supra), Mahkamah Rayuan telah menegaskan bahawa apabila terdapat dua set fakta yang bercanggah mengenai “custody” atau “control” dan percanggahan tersebut tidak dapat diselesaikan dengan alasan yang kukuh, manfaat keraguan hendaklah diberikan kepada OKT. Prinsip tersebut terpakai dengan dan relevan dalam kes semasa. (vi) Mahkamah mendapati bahawa Pendakwaan gagal membuktikan “custody” atau “control” OKT terhadap dadah tersebut pada tahap prima facie.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Azizan bin Md. Arshad

judgments.title: NG YOON SIEW & ors v UDA LAND (NORTH) SDN. BHD. & ors
judgments.catchwords: O.34 rule 1(5) and O.34 rule 6(1) of the Rules of Court 2012 (“ROC 2012”) – reinstatement of writ action - notwithstanding discretionary power of court to reinstate a suit, a litigant is not automatically entitled to reinstatement solely on the account of their solicitor's absolute negligence or carelessness - a sick certificate must explicitly state that the counsel is unfit to attend court - however, the submitted sick certificate explicitly states counsel is fit to attend court procedures thus wholly undermines counsel’s own arguments - permitting a sick certificate that explicitly declares an individual “fit to attend court procedures” to excuse an absence would set a dangerous precedent for the entire Malaysian legal system – it undermines the integrity of the medical evidence and amounts to an abuse of power and process - by overriding a professional diagnosis, the Court would effectively be seen as usurping the specialized domain of the medical profession - the Court must respect the explicit medical diagnosis as written.
judgments.judge: YA Dr Wendy Ooi Su Ghee

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v KANG HONG GUAN
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous drugs — Trafficking — 621.02 grams of Methamphetamine — Section 39B(1)(a) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Prima facie case — Evaluation of evidence at the close of the prosecution case. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Trial — Prima facie case — Section 180 Criminal Procedure Code — Maximum evaluation of evidence — Test for calling for defence — Whether evidence sufficient to warrant a conviction if the accused elects to remain silent — Application of the Balachandran, Looi Kow Chai, and Mohd Radzi Abu Bakar standards. EVIDENCE: Possession — Custody and control — Arrest away from the scene — Accused in possession of sole key and access card to apartment — Accused leading police to premises and unlocking door — Section 8 Evidence Act 1950 — Whether conduct establishes dominion over premises — Tenancy agreement — Admissibility and weight of unstamped, unsigned, and unverified tenancy document — Section 67 Evidence Act 1950 — Failure to prove due execution. CRIMINAL LAW: Dangerous drugs — Possession — Knowledge — Admissibility of cautioned statement — Section 37B(1)(b) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Failure to record precise words of caution — Impact on admissibility — Information leading to discovery — Section 27 Evidence Act 1950 — Information already known to police from physical clues (key tag and access card) — Whether discovery was the consequence of information supplied by accused — Application of the principle in PP v Basri Salihin [1993] 1 CLJ 420. EVIDENCE: Chain of custody — Integrity of exhibits — Unmarked exhibit — Clear plastic packet not itemised in search list, police report, or handover form — Failure of seizing officer to place identifying marks — Absence of clear photographic record — Reasonable doubt as to identity of exhibit — Exclusion of unmarked exhibit from proven quantity — Impact on aggregate weight of drugs. CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Charge — Amendment — Sections 158(1) and 173(h) Criminal Procedure Code — Reduction of drug weight in charge following exclusion of unmarked exhibit — Remaining weight (90.80 grams) still exceeding statutory threshold for trafficking presumption — Section 37(da)(xvi) Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 — Whether amendment causes prejudice to accused — Calling for defence on amended charge. EVIDENCE: Possession — Joint possession — Access by third parties — Evidence of co-occupants (brother and girlfriend) — Feminine items found at scene — Failure to investigate "real trafficker" arrested on same day — Whether exclusivity required for possession — Impact of investigative shortfalls (CCTV, DNA, fingerprints) on weight of prosecution case.

judgments.catchwords: Section 10(1) of the Arbitration Act 2005 - whether section 10(1) of the AA 2005 required the courts below to determine for themselves the existence and operability of the arbitration agreement, or whether that question ought to have been left to the arbitral tribunal under section 18 and the doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz - whether the 2nd Stay Application and OS 2 are barred by res judicata or issue estoppel arising from the April 2022 Decision - the proper construction of Clause 1.3 in its November 2019 form, and in particular whether it ever entitled the Appellant to commence arbitration against its own distributor - whether the June 2021 amendment to Clause 1.3 could, consistently with ordinary contractual principles, be applied retrospectively to a dispute that had already crystallised and was already the subject of litigation - whether the Appellant had, in any event, taken a step in the proceedings within the meaning of section 10(1), disentitling it to a stay - whether Clause 1.3 is void, in whole or in part, under sections 24 and 29 of the Contracts Act 1950, because it caps the Respondent’s recoverable damages - whether the Appellant’s unilateral right to appoint the sole arbitrator renders the arbitration agreement void, or offends natural justice - whether the finding that the Appellant acted in bad faith was properly made without a trial.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

parties.label: PLAINTIF
names: V Alakei A/p Veerapan (Sebagai Pentadbir Untuk Harta Pusaka Simati Muniandy A/l Sinnaiah)

judgments.catchwords: Trust - action for breach of trust arising from a trust deed, which has resulted in the Plaintiffs being deprived of their rightful beneficial shares in the proceeds from the sale of the land described in the instrument Photocopy document - secondary evidence in the form of photostat copies is admissible once the court is satisfied that a sufficient search has been conducted and the original documents cannot be found Trust elements - for a private express trust to be perfectly constituted, the ‘three certainties’, namely, certainty of intention, certainty of subject matter, and certainty of object, must be clearly established - a trust obligation is not extinguished by the death of a trustee, rather, it devolves upon his legal representatives or successors in title who take the property subject to the trust. Limitation Act 1953 - operation of s. 22(1)(b) hinges upon two essential prerequisites - first, the existence of a valid trust, and second, that the trust property or its proceeds remain in the possession of the trustee or were previously received and converted to its use Irrevocable power of attorney - contains an express declaration of irrevocability - although no monetary or tangible consideration passed between the parties, the fundamental purpose of the instrument was to empower the children to vindicate and protect their mother’s beneficial rights in the trust property - in the context of a familial proxy born out of physical necessity, that the absence of commercial consideration does not invalidate the mandate

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.title: MELODY CHONG WIN v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: This is an appeal by the appellant against the decision of the Sessions Court at Petaling Jaya convicting her of three offences under the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 (“DDA”), namely possession of 0.20 grams of nimetazepam under section 12 of the DDA, 15.59 grams of cannabis under section 6 of the DDA, and 0.15 grams of amphetamine under section 12 of the DDA. The learned Sessions Court Judge (“SCJ”) sentenced the appellant to ten months’ imprisonment on the first charge, one year’s imprisonment on the second charge, and ten months’ imprisonment on the third charge, all sentences to run concurrently from the date of arrest. Having heard the parties, I dismissed the appeal and affirmed the decision of the SCJ. The appellant has since appealed further to the Court of Appeal.
